findings.title: Agent bearer secret is sent to a signer URL read from the Pod, and the same secret also works at the gateway, so any Pod writer can capture it and act as that agent
findings.description: The new per-agent authentication uses one bearer secret. src/demo/environment.ts registers that same secret with both services (`gateway.enrollAgent(agentId, secretHash(s)); signer.enrollAgent(agentId, secretHash(s))`). The assistant sends it to `${wallet.signerEndpoint}/pay`, at src/agent/assistant.ts:196 and :254 and src/agent/checkoutPurchase.ts:153. `wallet` comes from `readWallet(this.cfg.pod, this.cfg.layout.wallet)`, which is Pod data. Only the gateway URL is fixed in the agent's config; the signer URL is not, and nothing checks it. So whoever can write the wallet document chooses where the agent sends its credential. That is exactly the adversary this same commit defends against in Ledger.observeRevision: an agent with Pod write access. In the demo every agent writes the Pod through the shared PodClient. With the captured secret the attacker is the victim agent at both the gateway and the signer, which undoes the commit's guarantees that a request is attributed to the agent whose secret it carries and that a credential goes only to the agent it was authorized for. It also contradicts the residual-risk text in src/trust/agentAuth.ts, which describes exposure only as plain HTTP on loopback or reading the agent's memory: the endpoint can be any host. The money impact is limited to the victim's mandates and the sellers they allow, but those mandates can be spent without authority and the victim's payment credentials, which work as bearer instruments at sellers, can be obtained.
findings.failureScenario: Reproduced on 514e078 with a script against startEnvironment and CSS. (1) A user-confirmed mandate lists only AGENT_1 as assignee. AGENT_2 calls /authorize on it with its own secret and gets 403 AGENT_NOT_AUTHORIZED. (2) AGENT_2 rewrites layout.wallet so sc:signerEndpoint points at a server it runs, which records the Authorization header and forwards to the real signer. (3) AGENT_1 makes an ordinary purchase. It returns `completed`, so nothing looks wrong, and AGENT_2's server has captured `Bearer sca_…`. (4) AGENT_2 sends that header to gateway /authorize on AGENT_1's mandate and gets 200, with an authorization naming urn:solid-commerce:agent:assistant-1. It then sends it to the real signer /pay and gets 200 with a payment credential.
findings.suggestedFix: Don't take the signer URL from the Pod for authenticated calls. Give ShoppingAssistant and CheckoutPurchaser a fixed signerUrl at setup, like gatewayUrl, and refuse, or at least never send the secret to, a wallet signerEndpoint that differs from it. Register separate secrets for the gateway and the signer, so a secret leaked at one service gives nothing at the other. Longer term, sign each request for its specific recipient (e.g. HTTP Message Signatures with a per-agent key) instead of sending a reusable bearer secret. Correct the agentAuth.ts residual-risk text either way.

findings.title: Revision pinning blocks the user's latest approved mandate with MANDATE_REVISION_CONFLICT, and the agent keeps reusing it
findings.description: Ledger.observeRevision (line 61) refuses any mandate whose signed text differs from one the gateway saw earlier at the same revision. Two different user-signed texts at revision 1 can come from the normal grounding flow. CommonGround.withRevision proposes revision 1 whenever no live record exists yet, and CommonGround.commit, for a proposal without `supersedes`, does `putTurtle(doc, ttl, existing ? {} : { ifNoneMatch: true })`: if the document now exists, it overwrites it unconditionally, with no ifMatch and no archive copy. If the gateway saw the first text before it was overwritten, it then refuses the live (latest) one. CommonGround finds nothing wrong with the live record, so a matching request reuses it and never proposes revision 2. Purchases under it fail every time until the terms change or validUntil passes. With a persistent ledgerPath this also survives gateway restarts. No money is lost, but a legitimately approved mandate stays unusable.
findings.failureScenario: Reproduced on 514e078. Two groundings of the same mandate slug ran before either was committed (two sessions or agents). Both proposed weatherreport-usdc revision 1, one with a 1 USDC limit and one with 2 USDC, and the user approved both. After the first commit, GET /budget returned 200, so the gateway had recorded r1. The second commit overwrote the document, and GET /budget then returned 403 MANDATE_REVISION_CONFLICT. The next grounding of the 2 USDC request gave 0 proposals and reused `weatherreport-usdc.ttl#it r1`. purchase() returned `blocked MANDATE_REVISION_CONFLICT a different signed text of revision 1 was seen before`, and does so on every retry.
findings.suggestedFix: In CommonGround.commit, write a proposal without `supersedes` only with ifNoneMatch. On a 412 (precondition failed), reload and propose existing.revision+1, archiving the existing record, rather than overwriting it. Also report a gateway MANDATE_REVISION_CONFLICT or MANDATE_SUPERSEDED back to grounding, so the agent proposes revision (gateway's highest seen)+1 instead of reusing the refused record.

findings.title: Rollback check refuses the user's own signed revisions when two proposals for one record id are committed (permanent lock-out, no attacker)
findings.description: commit() (line 316) copies whatever is live into `confirmed.supersedes` and never checks that the live document is still the revision the proposal was built on. The If-Match it sends uses the etag it read a moment earlier inside commit(), not the etag seen at load(). Preference and requirement ids are derived only from category + leftOperand (line 269), so one negotiate() can return two proposals with the same id, both at revision prev+1 and both naming history slot r(prev). This also happens when answer() returns a grounded preference that shares an id with a plain preference, or when two sessions or agents build on the same ctx. The first commit archives r(prev) and writes r(prev+1)a. The second commit then overwrites history slot r(prev) with r(prev+1)a, which is validly signed, and writes r(prev+1)b. The new load() check (lines 106-110) reads the revision from the signed content, finds revision prev+1 'archived as superseded' and refuses the live record as a rollback. Before this change (e4b6da3) the same flow loaded r(prev+1)b. Now nothing loads, and repeating the request repeats the refusal forever. Each retry goes to rev+2 (rev 4, then 6) and the second commit poisons the new slot the same way. Neither the earlier requirement nor the user's newly signed requirement or preference is in force, so prepare() purchases with no freshness constraint. The only trace is an 'Ignored ... rolled back' note that blames tampering.
findings.failureScenario: Reproduced on 514e078 with an in-memory Pod, the RuleInterpreter and an auto-approving ApprovalDevice. Session 1: 'Get me a Berlin weather report observed within 60 minutes.' commits requirement r1. Session 2: 'Get me a Berlin weather report observed within 30 minutes. I prefer reports observed within 10 minutes.' returns two proposals: requirement r2 and preference r2, both for preferences/weatherreport-observationageminutes.ttl#it with supersedes ...-r1.ttl. Both commit successfully. The next load() returns preferences: [] and ignored: 'rolled back: live revision 2 is not newer than signed revision 2 archived as superseded in .../history/weatherreport-observationageminutes-r1.ttl'. Sending the same request again proposes r4 and then r6, and each is refused the same way. The same script on e4b6da3 loads preference r2 with ignored: [].
findings.suggestedFix: In commit(), archive only when the live document is the revision being superseded: parse `existing` and require existing.revision === confirmed.revision - 1 (or carry the etag observed at load() in the proposal and use it as If-Match). Otherwise throw a conflict so the caller reloads and re-proposes. Also stop negotiate()/answer() from returning two proposals for the same record id at the same revision (merge them, or give requirement and preference distinct ids). Add a regression test for requirement + preference on the same property in one request.

findings.title: supersededUpTo is only computed for live records that verify, so re-approval after a tampered or deleted record is proposed as revision 1 and refused as a rollback
findings.description: load() runs highestArchived() only after the live document exists and its signature verifies (line 105 `continue`s first, and history slugs with no live document are never examined). So ctx.supersededUpTo stays empty for an id whose live record was tampered with or deleted, even though history holds validly signed revisions of it. The documented contract says supersededUpTo is 'per record id: the highest revision for which the history container holds a copy carrying a valid user signature'. withRevision() (lines 285-288) then finds neither `prev` nor `supersededUpTo` and returns revision 1 with no `supersedes`. commit() writes it over the bad or missing live document. The user signs it, and the next load() refuses it: 'rolled back: live revision 1 is not newer than signed revision 1'. The recovery path the change adds (propose n+2) is reached only for the rollback case, not for tamper or delete. The user's first legitimate re-approval is lost. Only a second approval, at revision n+2, sticks. For mandates the gateway separately refuses revision 1 as MANDATE_SUPERSEDED if it has seen a later revision.
findings.failureScenario: Reproduced on 514e078. Mandate r1 (1 USDC) is committed, then r2 (0.5 USDC), so history weatherreport-usdc-r1.ttl holds signed r1. Case A: an agent edits 0.5 to 50 in the live document, so load() reports 'terms changed after confirmation' and supersededUpTo = {}. Case B: an agent deletes the live document, again with supersededUpTo = {}. The user then says 'You may spend up to 0.5 USDC on weather reports from approved providers.' negotiate proposes revision 1, the user approves, and commit succeeds. The next load() has mandates: [] and ignored: 'rolled back: live revision 1 is not newer than signed revision 1 archived as superseded in .../history/weatherreport-usdc-r1.ttl' in both cases.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute the highest valid archived revision for every record id that has signed copies in history, independent of whether the live document exists or verifies. Run highestArchived before the signature `continue`, and scan history slugs that have no live document. Store it in supersededUpTo so withRevision() proposes max+2 in those cases too. Add tests for re-approval after a tampered and after a deleted live record.

title: x402 network, asset and EIP-712 domain in the challenge are not bound to the signed offer or the authorization; the signer signs whatever token and chain the challenge names

variantsStillOpen: Not budget reuse, but the L402 counterpart of this finding's card 'another resource' point. The gateway's L402 binding of invoice to offer and resource rests only on macaroon caveats that nobody verifies. offerBinding.ts:85-86 decodes them with macaroonCaveats() and never checks the HMAC. l402Terms (offerBinding.ts:87) returns resource: offer.resource, so the resource check at offerBinding.ts:128 can never fail for L402. reasoning:

Logs are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-solid-commerce/39c3ee22-1c47-5ae9-9392-934f16bed1a0/scratchpad/chk-l402rail/.

Original scenario: SAT mandate with totalLimit 25 and maxPerTransaction 25, TTL 2s. Each round authorizes challenge I1 with railReference I2, pays I1, reports payment_failed, waits for expiry and runs /reconcile. I ran 3 rounds per scheme.
- e4b6da3 (old.log): all 3 L402 rows were 'released' with ledger rail_reference = I2. The seller received 75 sat against a 25 sat mandate, and committed was back to 0. The card path did the same: pi_A was confirmed, pi_B was stored, 3 rows were released, the merchant got 15 and committed was 0. This confirms the finding.
- 514e078 (new.log): every round got 409 RAIL_REFERENCE_MISMATCH (offerBinding.ts:131-132). The signer was never called, the seller got 0, and committed stayed 0.

Why the fix holds:
- The rail reference now comes from the challenge itself. For L402 it is the decoded invoice's paymentHash, checked against the node's record (offerBinding.ts:79-87). For card it is the intent id, read from the PSP the gateway reconciles with; provider, status, amount, currency, merchant and resource must all match (offerBinding.ts:91-97, 128).
- That reference is signed into the authorization and stored as rail_reference (gatewayService.ts:174-180, 204). reconcileOne queries exactly that reference (gatewayService.ts:301-306).
- The signer refuses any challenge whose reference differs from auth.railReference: l402.ts:97 and cardPsp.ts:34. cardPsp.ts:38 also requires the intent's resource to match the authorization's. The signer refuses authorizations with no reference at all (signerService.ts:76).
- challengeDigest binds the challenge, so what the signer pays and what reconciliation asks about are now the same payment.

Close variants tried at 514e078, all blocked or harmless:
- V1, railReference left out: the gateway derives it and the row ends 'settled'. On old code this stored null and the row stayed 'pending'.
- V2, invoice string claiming 25 sat with the hash of a 1000-sat invoice: refused with OFFER_MISMATCH because the node's record differs. On old code it was authorized, and the signer paid the 1000-sat invoice.
- V4, an intent I created myself for the same merchant and price but another resource: refused with OFFER_MISMATCH. On old code it was authorized and paid.
- V5, an intent I created myself for the right resource: authorized and 'settled'. Money moved and was committed, so nothing was released.
- Reusing one invoice or intent across two transactions is refused once it is paid; if both are authorized before payment, both settle. That over-commits, so it is safe.

Expiry race (pay just before expiry, report failure just after; reconcileOne releases with no grace period, gatewayService.ts:293 and 310, while the signer checks expiry before its network calls, signerService.ts:82): 40 timed attempts gave 0 cases of released-but-paid. In the in-process simulator the payment always landed first. With real rail latency this window could exist, but it is a separate timing issue I did not reproduce, so I did not list it as open.

Regression test: I copied test/e2e.test.ts 'L402 and card: the gateway derives the rail reference from the challenge and binds it; the agent cannot swap it' unchanged into the e4b6da3 worktree. title: Agent identity is self-asserted and payment credentials are handed to any caller: unauthenticated GET /transactions/:id exposes the signed authorization, and the signer replays the credential to whoever presents it

The assistant then POSTs the gateway-signed authorization with `Authorization: Bearer <agent secret>` to whatever URL that file names (src/agent/assistant.ts:196, :254 recoverDelivery; src/agent/checkoutPurchase.ts:153). With the stolen secret it then got GET /transactions/:id 200, signer /pay 200 with replayed:true, and POST /authorize as AGENT_1 against AGENT_1's mandate 200 'authorized'. reasoning:
I wrote my own repro test and ran it in throwaway worktrees, all since removed. The main repo was never touched and is still on staging at 514e078 with a clean tree.

At 514e078 the original scenario no longer happens. AGENT_1 completed a real assistant purchase. An attacker process with no credentials then tried each step:

title: Vocabulary validation can be bypassed: criteria in statements with no category are never checked, and a quote in a value defeats the 'skip invalid statement' match
reasoning:
Verdict: fixed. Both bypasses are closed, I found no open variant, and the regression test fails on old code for the right reasons.

Original scenario, run with negotiate() on both commits:
- At e4b6da3 it reproduces. validateInterpretation reports only statement 3, and negotiate proposes both `requirement WeatherReport sellerIsMyFriend` and `preference WeatherReport bogus"`. The causes are the ones named in the finding:
  - the leftOperand check only runs when the statement has its own category (old interpretation.ts:59);
  - invalid statements are found with the greedy regex over error messages (old commonGround.ts:96);
  - negotiate later fills in the intention's category (old commonGround.ts:101).
- At 514e078 it no longer happens. Both statements are flagged (invalid = [1,2]) and nothing is proposed.

How the fix works:
- interpretation.ts:86-88 works out each statement's category: its own, else that of the latest valid intention before it.
- :92 rejects a criterion with no category anywhere.
- :93 checks leftOperand against that category, and :98 checks ambiguous-term candidates against the same one.
- :116-117 records invalid statements by index. Only a valid intention can set the inherited category.
- In commonGround.ts, negotiate calls checkInterpretation (:174), skips invalid statements by index (:180) and uses the category that was validated (:182). So validation and application cannot diverge.

Close variants: all were rejected at 514e078, and most were exploitable at e4b6da3.
- A statement with no category whose ambiguousTerm has a bogus candidate. Old code offered it as a question, and answering produced a meaning plus a requirement.
- The same with role=meaning.
- An explicit null category; an empty-string category.
- A later invalid intention (it does not change what later statements inherit).
- A Shoes intention followed by a WeatherReport-only property.
- A no-category statement before any intention.
- Quotes in both the text and the value; the same text as a valid statement plus a quote.
- A bogus operator or unit containing a quote.
- A leftOperand of `constructor` or `__proto__`.
- An existing agreed meaning plus a bogus candidate.

Controls still work: a valid no-category requirement still inherits WeatherReport and is proposed, and a valid statement that shares its text with an invalid one still goes through.

No regression for real interpreter output: the rule-based interpreter gives identical results on both commits for all 10 harness cases plus 5 extra phrasings, with no validation errors. The full suite at 514e078 passes: 128 of 128.

Regression test: run verbatim against e4b6da3's src, test/grounding.test.ts fails at load, because checkInterpretation is not exported there. With only that import made tolerant, all 5 tests in the 'vocabulary validation' suite fail with AssertionErrors:
- Test 3 gets proposals ['bogus"', 'sellerIsMyFriend'], which is exactly the original scenario.
- Test 4 drops the valid statement that shares its text with an invalid one.
- Tests 1 and 2 fail because the new errors are missing; test 1's scenario also produces a proposal on old code.
- Test 5 belongs to the separate per-purchase-limit fix.

Two nearby behaviours I did not count as open variants, because nothing outside the vocabulary reaches a proposal. Both are unchanged between the commits:
1. An authorization with no category and no valid intention gets the hard-coded target WeatherReport (commonGround.ts:215). checkInterpretation reports no category for it, so the "same rule negotiate() applies" comment does not fully hold for authorizations. WeatherReport is still in the vocabulary.
2. A statement whose category is a prototype key (for example `constructor`) makes validation throw at interpretation.ts:93, so nothing is proposed. The LLM schema's category enum (llmInterpreter.ts:48, enforced at jsonSchema.ts:65) keeps such values out.

Cleanup: both temporary worktrees are removed. /home/user/solid-commerce is clean, still on staging at 514e078. The scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-solid-commerce/39c3ee22-1c47-5ae9-9392-934f16bed1a0/scratchpad/vocab-repro/.

findings.title: The README's Terminal 2 proxy recipe fails when run as written: nothing waits for the proxy to start, and the test that claims to run the same commands waits for it
findings.description: README.md lines 159-165 start the proxy in the background (`npm run proxy -- --config proxy.example.json &`) and on the very next lines run `curl -i .../v1/aqi/current` (commented '# 402: x402, L402 and card challenges') and `npm run rails -- pay ...` (commented '# pays 8 SAT over L402: HTTP 200 with an sc-receipt'). Nothing waits for the proxy to listen, and tsx takes a few seconds to boot it. Line 167 says '`test/llm.test.ts` runs the same three commands with the real CLIs, on free ports.' It does not. The test spawns `node --import tsx src/...` directly instead of `npm run`. It waits for the proxy's 'unconfigured paths' banner before it sends any request, uses fetch instead of curl, and never runs `kill %1`. So the suite passes while the documented block fails. With a wait added the recipe does work at f851855 (checked with job control on): a 402 carrying PAYMENT-REQUIRED plus L402 and card-psp challenges, then 'paid 8 SAT over L402 (simulated); HTTP 200' with an sc-receipt, and `kill %1` stops the proxy.
findings.failureScenario: Reproduced at f851855 in a fresh worktree. Terminal 1 ran `npm run rails -- --example-upstream` (OK). The four Terminal 2 lines were run exactly as written, as a block (the way GitHub's copy button pastes them). Result: `curl: (7) Failed to connect to 127.0.0.1 port 8402 after 0 ms`. Then `npm run rails -- pay http://127.0.0.1:8402/v1/aqi/current` printed `fetch failed` and exited 1. The proxy's 'listening on http://127.0.0.1:8402' banner appeared only after both. Run without job control (as a script), `kill %1` signalled only the npm wrapper: the tsx and node proxy processes were left orphaned (PPID 1), still bound to 8402, and had to be killed by hand.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a readiness wait to the recipe after the `&` line, e.g. `until curl -sf -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8402/profile/card; do sleep 0.5; done`, or tell the reader to wait for the proxy's 'listening on' line before the next command. Reword line 167 to match what the test does ('the same steps, after waiting for the proxy to listen'), or make the test run the README block itself so it catches this.

findings.title: README's 'To add a scheme' steps are stale: they leave out the gateway's per-scheme challenge binder, so a scheme built from them is refused
findings.description: README.md line 25: 'To add a scheme, add a parser in `src/payments/http402.ts`, a payer in `src/signer`, a verifier in `src/payments/serverSide.ts` (used by the proxy), and a reconciler in the gateway.' findings.failureScenario: A developer adds a bank-initiation scheme by following the four listed steps exactly (parser, signer payer, proxy verifier, gateway reconciler). findings.title: llm-providers.md says the plain-http credential rule covers every provider, but the ClaudeInterpreter wrapper it recommends sends the key over plain http to any host

findings.failureScenario: Reproduced at f851855. title: Node floor ^22.13.0 || >=23.4.0 matches the first unflagged node:sqlite releases: fixed
reasoning:
The fix holds at f851855. Nowhere in the repo is the Node floor still set below the first release that loads node:sqlite without a flag.

What changed:
- package.json:37 and package-lock.json:29 (root entry): engines.node is now "^22.13.0 || >=23.4.0".
- README.md:31: "Requires Node.js ≥ 22.13 on the 22.x line, or ≥ 23.4 ...".
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:15: the matrix is ["22.13.0", "22"].
- A grep of all tracked files finds no other floor, no .nvmrc or .node-version, and no NODE_OPTIONS or --experimental-sqlite in any script.

Where the version boundary comes from:
1. Release binaries. I downloaded the official linux-x64 tarballs for 22.5.0, 22.12.0, 22.13.0, 23.3.0 and 23.4.0 and checked them against nodejs.org SHASUMS256 (all OK). The auto-mode classifier blocked running them, so I never executed them. Instead I read bin/node's bytes in memory and found the embedded setupSQLite() in pre_execution.js:
   - 22.5.0, 22.12.0 and 23.3.0: `if (!getOptionValue('--experimental-sqlite')) return;` (off unless the flag is passed).
   - 22.13.0 and 23.4.0: `if (getOptionValue('--no-experimental-sqlite')) return;` (on by default).
2. Changelogs. "unflag sqlite module" (#55890) is listed under "2025-01-07, Version 22.13.0 'Jod' (LTS)" in CHANGELOG_V22.md and under "2024-12-10, Version 23.4.0" in CHANGELOG_V23.md.
3. Semver. 22.12.0 and 23.3.0 fail the new range; 22.13.0, 23.4.0 and 24.0.0 satisfy it. No locked dependency has an engines.node that excludes 22.13.0 or 23.4.0.

The failure mode, on the installed Node 22.23.4:
- With NODE_OPTIONS=--no-experimental-sqlite, which turns on the same check that 22.5–22.12 apply by default, importing src/gateway/ledger.ts fails with ERR_UNKNOWN_BUILTIN_MODULE "No such built-in module: node:sqlite".
- Without it, the Ledger is created normally.
- Under the old docs (>=22.5) a 22.12 user met the requirement and hit this error. Under the new range they don't meet it.

The implementer's claim of "no API newer than 22.13" holds up as far as I checked:
- ledger.ts uses only the DatabaseSync constructor, exec, prepare, run, get and all, which have existed since 22.5. It does not use isOpen, columns, isTransaction, Symbol.dispose, iterate, function, aggregate or backup.
- Its SQL uses no math or JSON functions. That matters because 22.16 changed SQLite's compile flags ("enable common flags").
- The builtin modules it imports are long-standing APIs.
- Every 22.x release ships V8 12.4, so JavaScript language features cannot differ between 22.13 and 22.23.

Regression test (test/llm.test.ts:708):
- It passes at f851855.
- With e4b6da3's package.json, package-lock.json, README.md and ci.yml put back in a scratch worktree, it fails: AssertionError, expected '^22.13.0 || >=23.4.0', actual '>=22.5'.
- It only checks text in those files and does not exercise Node itself. The actual check against Node behaviour is the CI job on 22.13.0, which I could not run here.

Caveats, not open variants:
- I did not run the suite on exactly 22.13.0 or 23.4.0, because running downloaded binaries was blocked.
- engines is advisory. npm only warns with EBADENGINE, so a 22.12 user who ignores the warning still gets ERR_UNKNOWN_BUILTIN_MODULE. That is the intended outcome of raising the floor rather than adding the flag.
- 23.x and 24.x are not in the CI matrix, and the README does not claim they are.

I removed the scratch worktree (/tmp/chk-nodefloor-d7k2) after the checks, with its node_modules symlink deleted first. The main repo's status was clean and its node_modules intact.
